text:
The journey begins at the deck itself, the roadway that carries the actual traffic. The deck is not a flexible ribbon but a rigid steel or concrete girder, often stiffened with trusses, designed to spread the concentrated weight of a vehicle's tires across a wide area. Sitting directly above the deck, at regular intervals, hang the vertical suspender cables. These are in pure tension, acting like thousands of sturdy fingers reaching down to grasp the deck at every point along its length, taking the live load of traffic and the dead weight of the deck itself and hauling it upward. These suspender cables terminate at the great main cables overhead. A main cable is a marvel of engineering, not a single steel rod but a bundle of thousands of individual high-strength steel wires, compacted and wrapped into a single, unyielding rope. This main cable hangs in a specific curve between the towers, a catenary that becomes a parabola under uniform loading. As the suspender cables pull downward along the main cable's length, they create a massive tension along the entire cable. This tension is the key to carrying the load, because the deck is essentially hanging from the curve of the main cable, and the cable is trying to straighten out under that load, pulling the deck inward and upward. The shape of the curve is what elegantly transforms the purely downward force of the deck into both horizontal and vertical components of tension within the cable itself.

The path of this tension now splits at the towers. The main cable passes over a large saddle mounted atop each tower. The saddle transfers the vertical component of the cable's force straight down into the tower columns. The towers are in pure compression; they are massive, rigid structures that press directly downward into their foundations and anchor bolts, pushing that vertical load straight into the ground below. However, the horizontal component of the cable tension cannot be handled by the towers. If the towers tried to resist this horizontal pull, they would simply tip over. Instead, the horizontal tension is allowed to pass right over the saddle, up and over, and continues down the other side of the tower toward the ends of the bridge. At the ends, this horizontal tension becomes the most critical part of the load path. There, the main cables are splayed out into individual strands and anchored into enormous concrete blocks called anchorages or gravity anchorages. These blocks are massive, often weighing thousands of tons, and are buried deep into bedrock or massive concrete footings. The entire horizontal tension of the main cables is pulled directly into these anchorages. Because the anchorage is so heavy and so securely fixed to the earth, the ground itself provides the necessary reaction force; the cable pulls on the concrete, but the concrete's weight and its friction with the soil resist that pull, effectively transferring the load into the ground. In some cases, inclined tunnels are bored into solid rock, and the cables are anchored deep inside, gripping the rock with steel rods.

Thus, the complete path is resolved. The truck on the deck pushes down, forcing the deck to bend, but the suspender cables grab it and transfer that force as tension into the main cable. The main cable's geometry forces this tension to have distinct vertical and horizontal parts. The vertical part pushes down through the towers into the ground, while the horizontal part pulls outward to the ends and is anchored into the earth by gravity and friction. Every single load on the bridge is ultimately resolved into compression on the towers and tension on the anchorages, both of which the planet's crust easily absorbs.
